title: Cyrus and the Silence
premise: Tamsin Thackeray has spent nine years mailing postcards to the charred address of a house in Marrow Bend, writing to a mother whose memory is dissolving into dementia — and whose silence Tamsin once chose over testifying against the man who burned the place down. When a radio plays a song Tamsin's mother wrote and never recorded, sung under a stranger's name, the grief Tamsin has curated into polite smiles finally cracks open. Following the song's trail, Tamsin uncovers a web of stolen songs, bought silence, and a brother who took the blame they never earned. The story ends with Tamsin testifying at last — not to a court, but to their mother, reading the postcards aloud in a care home sunroom as the truth, and the song, finally belong to the right people.
about_author: Jonah Reyes is the pen name of a former small-town radio archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsung local songwriters before turning to fiction. Cyrus and the Silence is their second novel, following a well-reviewed debut about a lighthouse keeper's letters.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. We meet Tamsin at the post office, mailing postcard #412 to a burned address, deflecting a coworker's kindness with practiced charm. The chapter establishes the ritual, the wit as armor, and the dread of Sunday visits to a mother who no longer knows their name. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as composure.

chapters.title: A Song on the Frequency
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Driving home, a late-night radio program plays a haunting ballad — 'Cyrus' Lament' — credited to a songwriter named Dell Harrow. Tamsin pulls over, shaking: it is their mother's song, the one she sang only once and swore never to record. Beat: the past knocking loudly on a door Tamsin sealed.

chapters.title: Sunday, Room 9
chapters.summary: Alternating Tamsin's present POV with fragments of the mother's dissolving interiority. Tamsin visits Iris Thackeray, who mistakes Tamsin for her late husband and hums three bars of the song without knowing why. Tamsin says nothing about the radio. Beat: guilt compounding; time running out in a measurable way.

chapters.title: Marrow Bend, Before
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Tamsin's memory at nineteen: the house, the fire, the police station, and the moment Tamsin stayed silent while their brother Cyrus took the fall. We learn the fire was no accident and that Iris saw who did it — and stopped speaking afterward. Beat: the original wound, shown whole.

chapters.title: The Man Who Sings Other People's Grief
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin tracks Dell Harrow to a dive gig two towns over and confronts him afterward. Dell is defensive, then frightened: he bought the song in good faith from a publisher, Kestrel Music, who told him it was an estate sale. Beat: first ally or first liar — Tamsin can't tell.

chapters.title: Kestrel Music Has No Kestrels
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin visits the Kestrel Music offices and meets Vivian Okonkwo, a junior archivist who quietly confirms the 'estate sale' paperwork is forged — Iris Thackeray never signed anything. Vivian warns Tamsin off; the owner, Roland Kestrel, has ruined people before. Beat: the enemy acquires a name and a lobby.

chapters.title: Letters to a Burned House
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, intercut with the postcards themselves — nine years of them, reproduced in full. The chapter traces how Tamsin's voice changed from rage to apology to something like prayer, and reveals a single postcard that was returned unopened, marked 'addressee unknown.' Beat: grief as correspondence with no reply.

chapters.title: Cyrus Comes Home
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, his first in the book. Paroled two years ago, Cyrus has been living quietly as a carpenter, refusing contact with the family that abandoned him. He hears the same radio broadcast and recognizes the song instantly. Beat: the wronged brother re-enters the story on his own terms.

chapters.title: The Parking Lot Truce
chapters.summary: Alternating Tamsin and Cyrus POVs. They meet by chance — or Dell's arrangement — outside Iris's care home. Nine years of silence between siblings compressed into one bitter, funny, devastating conversation. Cyrus agrees to help, but only if Tamsin admits why they never spoke up. Beat: the truce is real and conditional.

chapters.title: What Iris Saw
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Cyrus's joint investigation. A neighbor from the old street, Mrs. Adeyemi, reveals that Iris witnessed Roland Kestrel's enforcer torch the house after Iris refused to sell her song catalog — and that Iris's silence afterward was not dementia but a bargain: her quiet for Cyrus's safety. Beat: the mother's silence reframed as sacrifice, not weakness.

chapters.title: The Archive in the Attic
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the ruins-adjacent storage unit Iris kept, the siblings find her original notebooks: forty songs, dated, signed, and a 1998 contract Kestrel forged. Also a photograph of Tamsin at nineteen, on the back of which Iris wrote: 'Tell them. Or tell no one. But choose.' Beat: evidence and indictment in one box.

chapters.title: Dell's Confession
chapters.summary: Dell's POV. Dell admits he suspected the catalog was stolen years ago and looked away because Kestrel made his career. He offers to testify, then wavers when Kestrel's lawyer sends a photo of Dell's daughter's school. Beat: the cost of conscience made concrete; an ally's courage tested.

chapters.title: The Cease-and-Desist
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Kestrel Music serves Tamsin with legal threats, digs up Cyrus's parole conditions, and lets Tamsin know Iris's care home funding traces back to a Kestrel 'charity.' The threat is elegant: speak up, and your mother loses her bed. Beat: rising tension — the enemy weaponizes Tamsin's own duty of care.

chapters.title: The Smile Fails
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At a benefit where Kestrel appears as a beloved patron of songwriters, Tamsin is introduced to him and cannot perform composure. The scene ends with Tamsin publicly accusing him, shaking, in front of a room that chooses to laugh. Beat: humiliation as turning point — the armor breaks, and something freer appears beneath.

chapters.title: Room 9, Again
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Cyrus's POV, shared. They play Iris the recording of her own song. For ninety seconds she is entirely present — she names the song, names the night of the fire, names Kestrel — then recedes. Cyrus weeps; Tamsin finally understands what the postcards were for. Beat: a lucid window that is both gift and deadline.

chapters.title: Vivian's Decision
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. She copies Kestrel's forged contracts, the enforcer's payments, and a ledger of a dozen other stolen catalogs, and mails them to the siblings — knowing she will be fired and possibly sued. Beat: the quiet archivist becomes the story's conscience; the case becomes bigger than one family.

chapters.title: The Other Families
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Following Vivian's ledger, Tamsin and Cyrus visit three other families Kestrel robbed: a gospel singer's widow, a blues guitarist, a dead man's son. Each adds testimony; each also warns how Kestrel destroyed the last people who tried. Beat: private grief becomes collective; the stakes widen.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with Cyrus present. On the eve of the hearing Kestrel's lawyer forced by countersuing them, Tamsin writes postcard #413 — the first addressed to a living person, delivered by hand to Room 9. Cyrus and Tamsin reconcile the old silence: Tamsin finally says the words they owed. Beat: stillness before the storm; forgiveness not granted but begun.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs in sequence: Tamsin testifying, Cyrus corroborating, Vivian presenting the ledger, Dell arriving despite the photograph of his daughter, Mrs. Adeyemi describing the fire. Kestrel's lawyer unravels on the forged signature. Beat: the climax — justice pursued inside the law at last, won by ordinary, terrified people.

chapters.title: What the Law Can't Return
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Kestrel settles rather than faces criminal referral; the catalogs revert, but no verdict restores nine years. Cyrus declines a settlement windfall, asking instead that the songs be reissued under Iris's name. Dell records 'Cyrus's Lament' properly, crediting Iris Thackeray. Beat: bittersweet accounting — victory that is real and insufficient.

chapters.title: The Sunroom
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin reads all 413 postcards aloud to Iris over one long afternoon in the care home sunroom. Iris surfaces briefly, pats Tamsin's hand, and hums the song's final line — the one she never finished. Tamsin finishes it for her. Beat: the emotional resolution; love spoken directly at last, duty and love reconciled.

chapters.title: Coda: The Address That Isn't Burned
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV, months later. The Marrow Bend house lot, bought with the settlement, hosts a small recording studio and songwriters' retreat bearing Iris's name. Tamsin mails one last postcard — to the new address, where someone will answer. The radio plays the song; this time, her name follows it. Beat: identity reclaimed; silence turned into song.
